ex: If you have a feature request, a new integration idea, or you would like to file a bug report, please use this Github issue tracker. Feel free to drop in a line wherever it is easiest for you.

hn-50352757.t: OpenAI seems to be silently re-enabling model training on Codex chats
hn-50352757.s: My company is pretty paranoid about leaking IP to the frontier labs through prompts, so we've all been diligent about disabling data sharing in Codex/Claude Code/etc.
ex: My company is pretty paranoid about leaking IP to the frontier labs through prompts, so we've all been diligent about disabling data sharing in Codex/Claude Code/etc. But yesterday my coworkers and I noticed that the setting had been silently reenabled in Codex. None of us knowingly opted back in. You can check your settings here: https://chatgpt.com/settings/data-controls. Look for "Improve the model for everyone". Curious if this is an isolated issue or something more widespread. EDIT: looks like this has been noted before https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49643556 EDIT: apparently you can also turn off data sharing here: https://privacy.openai.com/policies?modal=take-control

hn-50351111.t: The 'Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen' post is misleading
hn-50351111.s: The experiments that read raw weights and the ones that fix Qwen use completely different techniques.
ex: Stage magicians often do the same trick multiple ways. One iteration uses a gimmick prop, the next one shows you the prop isn’t gimmick but that one palms the object, the third time was a forced choice etc. When you watch the performance you assume there’s only one technique, so each time they do it they seem to debunk your hypothesis about how it must be working. This is pretty much how the experiments in the ‘Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen’ post work. The post’s abstract says: Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights.

hn-50344919.t: The SEC Should Block Anthropic's IPO to Protect the Public
hn-50344919.s: If Anthropic goes public, workers, retail investors, and retirees will be left holding the bag when its bills come due, writes Matt Scherer.
ex: Matt Scherer is co-author of the recent report Brace for Impact: Protecting people and the economy when the AI bubble bursts. Things are seldom what they seem when it comes to the finances of the AI industry. The AI ecosystem’s circular business dealings, extensive use of financial engineering, and otherwise murky finances make it hard for investors, regulators, or workers saving for retirement to get an accurate financial picture of AI companies. That is particularly true of Anthropic, which filed the registration statement for its initial public offering (IPO) last week ahead of a planned November stock market debut. The company’s topline financial figures look quite impressive for a startup, with revenues that appear to have grown quickly over the course of 2026 and a fairly healthy balance sheet — on the surface, that is. Dig a little deeper, however, and a far bleaker picture emerges.

hn-50355251.t: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
hn-50355251.s: Yesterday’s hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab.
ex: Yesterday’s hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a “blog post”, but it’s paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model—literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I’ve been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I’m delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well! Here’s the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights: Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do.

hn-50348962.s: Auto Ontology is a Python framework for building semantic, graph-based reasoning layers over data. It enables deterministic query generation, better context retrieval, and more explainable AI for LLM…
ex: Agents can retrieve documents and query databases, but reliability gates agentic analytics: a revenue metric answered faster is worth nothing if the number is wrong. Agents need a context layer that tells them where data lives, what it means, whether to use it, how to use it, where it came from, and what is similar. NVIDIA Auto Ontology is an open library that builds that layer from enterprise metadata, reconciles definitions across systems, and exposes it to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. It complements the semantic models customers already own. - Discover: generate enterprise ontologies from metadata; connect existing ontologies and semantic models; build AI-ready knowledge graphs. - Ground: give agents trusted business meaning for metrics, entities, and relationships; reconcile inconsistent definitions across systems. - Validate: check generated queries against certified definitions and lineage; return provenance with every answer.

hn-50354358.t: Stringman, an $800 open-source room scale gripper robot
hn-50354358.s: In robotics, price is basically actuator count. Stringman reaches an entire room with four motors, hanging its gripper from lines anchored in the ceiling corners.
ex: In robotics, price is basically actuator count. Stringman reaches an entire room with four motors, hanging its gripper from lines anchored in the ceiling corners. Working from above, it reaches floors too cluttered for any wheeled or legged robot. And since the lifting force is shared by all motors, payload capacity scales with their combined torque instead of a single actuator's, peaking near the center of the room where the lines share the load most evenly. *0.75 m serial arm using the same DM-H6215 1 N·m direct drive actuators at rated torque, ignoring the weight of its own links. Stringman figure is for a 7 × 7 × 3 m room at the 28 N line tension limit, net of its 638 g gripper and marker. Stringman is open source and OSHWA certified. The mechanical CAD, the PCBs, and the control software are all published. We believe owners should be in control of their own robots.

hn-50344861.t: LLMs are not superhuman at reading and writing neural network weights
hn-50344861.s: A recent paper argues that frontier LLMs can work with neural network weights directly. This seems superhuman, but it isn’t.
ex: A recent paper argues that frontier LLMs can work with neural network weights directly. This seems superhuman, but it isn’t. The paper shows that GPT-6 Astra can take a small neural network and interact with its weights directly, “well past what we’d expect from humans or conventional algorithms”. Specifically, Astra was able to identify what games a small network1 was trained to play just by looking at the weights, and even tweak the weights itself. The most impressive result is Astra significantly improving a 0.8B Qwen LLM’s ability on mathematics by natively editing its weights. The reason to be excited here is that “superhuman ability to improve language models” is precisely the kind of thing that could cause recursive self-improvement. I think a smart human ML researcher could perform all of these tasks.

hn-50346153.t: Intel stock collapse worsens as $3.5T chip rout spreads
hn-50346153.s: Intel's slide spread through memory and storage stocks Monday as most of Wall Street moved on from last week's tech sell-off.
ex: Wall Street mostly swept up last week's tech wreckage Monday. Chip stocks kept tracking mud back through the house. About 7 in 10 S&P 500 stocks rose Monday, yet nearly every chip stock fell, and the group shed more than $400 billion in market value in a single session, by Yahoo Finance calculations. The chipmaker slid about 9% after its worst day since 1974 on Oct. 30, when a disappointing forecast knocked nearly 29% off the stock. Monday's close left Intel worth less than half of what it was when September ended. Micron (MU), Sandisk (SNDK), Seagate (STX), and Western Digital (WDC) — the memory and storage names that led the chip boom this year — all got clobbered, falling roughly 6% to 8%. Marvell (MRVL) fell even harder, a drop that came as it agreed to buy Lumentum (LITE) in a $115 billion deal. Nvidia (NVDA) held up better than most, but it's still down about 16% since Oct. 6. Zoom out and the mess gets bigger.

hn-50336918.t: Fujifilm to boost tape production 5x as AI fuels archiving demand
hn-50336918.s: Low costs and offline security mean magnetic tape still has a job.
ex: In an announcement released Thursday, Fujifilm said it will invest roughly 10 billion yen (about $63 million) to increase its production capacity fivefold for an unlikely beneficiary of the AI era: magnetic tape. Fujifilm attributes the surge in archiving demand to the spread of generative AI, which the company remarked is producing “exponential growth” in data needs worldwide. The 5x increase in production capacity will be measured against fiscal year 2025 production levels. The investment in Fujifilm’s Kanagawa Factory, Odawara site will make it “the largest investment Fujifilm has made to date in dedicated LTO tape facilities.” The project will run from fiscal years 2026 through 2028 to fund manufacturing expansion and additional personnel, primarily to produce the latest-generation “FUJIFILM LTO Ultrium10” tape. Mainstream consumers may have abandoned tape decades ago, but the enterprise world never did. Cloud giants rely on tape to back up vast troves of data.

hn-50334038.t: China's First Frontier AI Export Controls: Mofcom Announcement No. 48
hn-50334038.s: On October 16, 2026, China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) and Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST) issued Announcement No. 48 of 2026.
ex: On October 16, 2026, China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) and Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST) issued Announcement No. 48 of 2026. The announcement proposes adding 40 technologies to the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export, 23 of them in artificial intelligence, and it imposes an interim pre-export registration requirement that is already in effect [1][2]. China’s catalogue has touched AI before: the 2020 revision added personalized recommendation and AI interaction interface technology [6]. Unlike those 2020 additions, the draft reaches frontier model weights, agent architectures, and AI-enabled offensive cyber capability, with explicit technical thresholds for each [1]. The announcement contains two instruments with different legal status. The catalogue additions are a draft open for comment until November 15, 2026, while the registration requirement applies now, including to exports that have started but are not yet complete [1][2].
